title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close reading of what many consider Dickens's most ambitious, most unsettling, and most modern novel.

I'm your host, and over this series we'll be living inside the world Dickens created in 1864 and 1865 — a world built on a dust heap and shot through with questions about money, identity, and what it means to be truly human.
This opening episode takes up the novel's central obsession: the relationship between money and moral worth.
To dig into that, I'm joined by three wonderful readers and thinkers — each of whom brings something quite distinct to this novel.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose life's work has been the moral imagination of the great novelists.
Edmund reads Dickens as a storyteller of character and conscience — and he'll keep us honest when we're tempted toward purely political readings.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what the institutions Dickens depicts actually looked like from the inside.
He'll tell us what a dust contractor's fortune really meant in 1860s London — and why it mattered who inherited it.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has been returning to it ever since.
Caroline brings the reader's eye — the sense of what is funny, what is devastating, and what makes you stop and read a sentence twice.
So — Our Mutual Friend opens on the Thames at night, a man and a girl dragging corpses from the river for whatever can be scavenged from the bodies.
It's not a gentle beginning.
Edmund, I want to start with you — what does Dickens announce about this novel's moral universe in those very first pages?
What Dickens announces, I think, is that value and filth are inseparable in this world — that there is no fortune untouched by something degrading.
Old John Harmon — old Dust — has built his entire estate by sifting through what other people threw away.
The dust heaps are not merely a colourful Victorian detail.
They are the novel's founding image of inherited wealth — something that smells, that must be sifted through, before one can possess it decently.
Dr. Johnson observed that a man who has money has a great advantage, but a man who deserves it has a greater one still.
Dickens is asking, from the very first chapter, whether the two can ever coincide.
And Gaffer Hexam — the river dredger — is a brilliant opening figure, because he insists on a moral distinction that the novel immediately holds up to scrutiny.
He will not rob the living, he says — only the dead.
It is a distinction that tells us everything about how this novel uses respectability as a form of self-deception.
James, you've spent years inside the actual machinery of Victorian inheritance law and poor relief.
Does Dickens get that machinery right — and does it matter?
He gets it right in the ways that count — the emotional and social logic of it.
Old Harmon's will — the condition that his son must marry a woman the father has selected, or forfeit everything — was entirely enforceable under mid-Victorian testamentary law.
The idea that a dead man's preferences could govern a living person's intimate choices — that was not Dickensian exaggeration.
That was the ordinary operation of property law.
What strikes me about the novel's opening is the sheer density of different economies it introduces almost simultaneously.
You have the river economy — Gaffer and Lizzie dredging bodies for rewards.
You have the dust heap inheritance — old Harmon's accumulated filth-money.
And within pages you have the Veneerings — new money performing old money with a desperation that is practically audible.
Dickens understood that money is never just money — it is always also a story you tell about yourself.
That line about the Veneerings is exactly where I want to start — because for me, the Veneering dinner party chapters are some of the most dazzling writing in the entire novel.
Dickens introduces the Veneerings with this description of their furniture and possessions as things that have no past — everything is new, new, new.
"Mr. and Mrs. Veneering were bran-new people in a bran-new house in a bran-new quarter of London."
That triple repetition — bran-new, bran-new, bran-new — is Dickens performing newness until it becomes absurd.
It's hilarious and it's savage at the same time.
And the Veneerings' guests — this rotating cast of London society figures — they barely have names.
Twemlow, the Buffers, Boots and Brewer — they are types, cogs in the machinery of social pretension.
What Edmund said about self-deception — I think the Veneerings embody that perfectly.
They don't just have money; they have assembled, at great expense, the appearance of having always had money.
Caroline is right about the verbal music — and I'll confess I find those Veneering chapters among the most technically accomplished satirical writing in the language.
But I want to preserve a distinction that I think the novel is carefully making.
The Veneerings are contemptible not because they are nouveaux riches — Dickens is not a snob in that crude sense.
They are contemptible because they have confused the symbol of worth with worth itself.
Burke — and Dickens would not have disowned the comparison — understood that a society's manners and its morals are bound together.
When you lacquer everything in veneering, you have destroyed the connection between surface and substance.
And that, not mere ostentation, is what Dickens finds truly dangerous.
I want to add something to that from the historical side, because the timing of this novel matters enormously.
Dickens is writing in the early 1860s — a moment of extraordinary financial speculation in Britain.
Railway mania had already come and gone, but the City was still churning with joint-stock companies and paper fortunes.
Veneering is not just a satirical figure — he is a recognisable type to Dickens's first readers.
The man who arrived from nowhere with a City fortune and bought his way into society — that was the anxiety of the age.
And what makes the novel so interesting is that Dickens does not simply condemn this — he shows us how the old money is no better.
The Wilfer household, the Lammles, the Podsnaps — every layer of English society is touched by this corruption.
Podsnap — now there's a creation I find both brilliant and personally exhausting to read.
He's the figure who has decided, once and for all, that everything in England is perfect and anything that suggests otherwise is simply not done.
Dickens gives him this magnificent gesture — the arm sweeping away all unpleasant facts, brushing them off the face of the earth.
It's such a precise comic image for a particular kind of willed ignorance.
And what I find moving — and this connects to everything we've been saying — is that Lizzie Hexam exists in complete contrast to all of this.
She has nothing — no money, no position, a father who is morally compromised and socially despised.
And yet from the first chapter she radiates a kind of moral clarity that none of the dinner party guests can approach.
That tension — between those who have wealth and perform goodness, and those who have neither and embody it — is, for me, the beating heart of this novel.
That opposition — performance versus embodiment of goodness — will run through everything we discuss today.
After the break, we'll turn to the river itself — the Thames as both literal setting and moral landscape.
And we'll look closely at what Dickens does with drowning, rebirth, and the man who becomes a stranger to himself.

segments.title: The Machinery of Ruin: Law, Poverty, and the Dust Heaps

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been exploring the novel's extraordinary surface — its Thames, its grotesques, its love plots.
But now we turn to what lies underneath: the machinery of ruin that Dickens builds into the very structure of his world.
Law, poverty, and the dust heaps — three forces that grind people down, or sometimes, remarkably, lift them up.
Sir Edmund, let me begin with you — because you've always resisted the reading of Dickens as primarily a social campaigner.
Does the dust heap world force you to revise that view at all?
It does not force me to revise it, no — though I confess the dust heaps present a particular challenge to one's composure.
What Dickens has done with old Harmon's mounds is something more interesting than political allegory.
He has made filth into fortune — and then asked whether fortune is anything other than filth.
That is a moral question, not a sociological one.
Consider Boffin — the Golden Dustman, as he is called.
His goodness is not explained by the dust heaps, nor corrupted by them — not permanently, at any rate.
It is his character that matters. The money is merely the test.
I have great respect for that reading, Edmund, but I think it lets the novel off a hook that Dickens himself hammered in.
The dust heaps were real. Dickens's readers knew exactly what they were looking at.
London's dust yards — the sorting grounds for cinders, bones, rags, human waste — were a genuine industry in the 1860s.
The fortunes they generated were, in the most literal sense, built on what the city threw away.
And what the city threw away, of course, included people.
Think of Betty Higden — she is the human correlate to the dust.
She runs herself to death across the countryside rather than enter the workhouse.
That is not a metaphor for the Poor Laws — it is a direct, unsparing representation of what they did to people.
What I keep coming back to is the scene where Betty actually voices her terror.
She speaks of the Poor Law with this visceral, almost animal dread.
Dickens gives her the line — and I am paraphrasing very closely here — that she would sooner trust herself to the river than to the parish.
And the terrible irony is that the river has already taken John Harmon — or so everyone believes.
The novel is saturated with this double meaning around water — cleansing, drowning, resurrection, disposal.
And against all that water — this dry, suffocating mountain of dust.
Caroline is right that the novel saturates everything in elemental imagery — and that is precisely my point.
Dickens is working mythically, not programmatically.
The dust heap is the underworld. The river Styx flows through Southwark.
Rogue Riderhood and Gaffer Hexam are not merely economic figures — they are chthonic ones.
And the law — Mr. Tulkinghorn is in Bleak House, I know, but the Veneering world serves the same function here.
Lawyers, Chancery proceedings, the interminable Harmon will — they are the grinding machinery that keeps inheritance just out of reach.
The Harmon will is a beautifully observed piece of legal theatre, I'll grant that.
Dickens understood the Courts of Chancery and the rules of testamentary succession quite precisely by this point in his career.
The condition attached to the Harmon fortune — that John must marry a girl he has never met or lose everything — is not a Gothic invention.
Conditional bequests of exactly this kind were entirely legal and were regularly enforced.
So when young Harmon decides to disappear — to test whether Bella Wilfer is worth having on honest terms — he is essentially staging a legal fiction inside a legal fact.
Dickens rather enjoys that paradox.
And Bella's arc is so precisely calibrated to that legal and financial world.
She begins the novel as someone who openly, almost defiantly, wants to be rich.
She says — and this is quite early in the book — that she is mercenary, and that she is not ashamed of it.
There's something wonderfully honest about that.
She has grown up in a cramped little house in Holloway, bequeathed to a dead man's family as a kind of footnote in a will.
Of course she wants money. The novel doesn't condescend to her for it.
What it does is take her through fire — through Boffin's performed miserliness, through Rokesmith's patient love — until she understands what money costs.
That performance of Boffin's — the feigned miserliness — is one of the great structural gambles of the novel.
Many readers — and I confess I was among them on first reading — take it at face value for rather too long.
We believe Boffin has been corrupted by the dust heap fortune, as any moralist might predict.
And then Dickens pulls the curtain back and reveals that Boffin has been protecting Bella all along.
That is a moral surprise — not a social one. It vindicates the goodness that was always latent in the character.
Burke would say that character formed over a lifetime resists the accidents of fortune.
I'm willing to enjoy that as narrative — it is enormously satisfying as narrative.
But we should be honest that it is also a kind of fairy tale resolution to a very real problem.
In the real 1860s, dust yard fortunes did not come with a Boffin who secretly ensures the poor are protected.
What they came with was Silas Wegg — the opportunist, the parasite — circling the mounds.
Wegg is the most accurate figure in the novel, frankly.
A man without scruple, without skill, without claim — but with a talent for attaching himself where money might be.
Wegg is also extraordinarily funny — and I think Dickens needs that comedy to survive the darkness around him.
His recitations of Decline and Fall — getting it magnificently wrong — are pure music-hall.
But when he tries to blackmail Boffin with the second will he's discovered in the mounds — the comedy curdles.
Suddenly this pantomime villain is actually dangerous, actually grasping, actually representative of something.
The dust heaps contain multiple wills — multiple versions of how wealth might be disposed.
That is an extraordinary image for a novel about inheritance and identity — everything buried, everything waiting to be found.
And let us not lose sight of the Lammles and the Veneerings — because they represent a different mechanism of ruin entirely.
The Veneering dinner table is where new money performs its legitimacy — where City fortunes buy social position.
And Dickens's satire there is absolutely merciless — these people have no inner life, only surface.
The name itself — Veneering — does half the work before a word is spoken.
And Dickens makes the Lammles' marriage — two people who each thought the other was rich and discover neither is — into a kind of capitalist tragedy.
They then proceed to survive by fraud — by preying on others — because the system offers them no other instrument.
I would not argue with that — the Veneering world is Dickens at his most withering.
There is a passage where the Veneerings are described as having everything new about them — new house, new furniture, new friends — and Dickens writes it with this magnificent, deadpan accumulation.
The effect is that newness itself becomes a kind of vulgarity — a confession of having no past worth mentioning.
Burke would have understood that perfectly.
Society without inheritance — without the weight of the past — becomes mere competition for glittering surfaces.
What strikes me reading those Veneering chapters is the role of Twemlow.
This mild, impoverished gentleman who keeps being deployed as a kind of social prop — the one person at the table with genuine ancestry.
And at the very end of the novel, Twemlow speaks.
He defends Eugene Wrayburn's marriage to Lizzie Hexam against all the social machinery of the table.
He says — quietly, definitively — that a gentleman is one who acts with gentleness and honour, whatever his station or hers.
It is one of the novel's most quietly radical moments — and Dickens gives it to the least powerful person in the room.
And that image of Twemlow — the spent gentleman, the last honest voice at the Veneering table — brings us back to where we started.
The machinery of ruin in this novel is not only the dust heaps or the Poor Law or the Harmon will.
It is the entire social arrangement — the dinner tables, the wills, the rivers — everything that determines who matters and who is thrown away.
And yet Dickens — perhaps despite himself — keeps imagining people who refuse to be ground down by it.
Next, we turn to one of those people — and to the remarkable language Dickens finds to describe the Thames at night.

segments.title: Bella's Appetite: Reading a Woman's Desires

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've spent time with the Thames, with dust heaps, with the elaborate machinery of inheritance.
Now we turn to one of the novel's most fascinating and, I'd argue, most modern characters: Bella Wilfer.
Bella wants things — openly, cheerfully, without apology.
She wants money, comfort, a better life than the Wilfer household provides.
And Dickens, remarkably, doesn't punish her for wanting — at least not straightforwardly.
Edmund, you've always had strong views on Bella as a moral case study.
Where do you begin with her?
Bella Wilfer is, I think, the most psychologically honest portrait of feminine ambition in all of Victorian fiction.
And I say that as someone deeply suspicious of readings that flatten character into social symptom.
Bella's great declaration early in the novel — that she is 'a hideous little mercenary wretch' — is the key to everything.
'I am something of a doll, I know, a thing made to be played with and shown off.'
The self-awareness there is extraordinary — she is diagnosing her own condition before anyone else in the novel has the wit to do so.
Now, Dr. Johnson would say that a character who sees their own vice clearly is already halfway to virtue.
The question is whether Dickens trusts her enough — whether he gives her the space to complete that journey on her own terms.
That self-diagnosis is what I fell in love with as a young reader, and it hasn't dimmed at all for me.
Most heroines of the period are good in spite of poverty; Bella is openly discontented because of it.
There's that wonderful scene early on where she surveys the cramped Wilfer parlour and simply refuses to be reconciled to it.
And Dickens writes her impatience with such relish — you can feel him enjoying her.
What moves me is the dinner scene with her father — where Rumty Wilfer takes her to Greenwich.
She is so hungry — not just for food, but for pleasure, for warmth, for being treated as someone who matters.
And Dickens lets that hunger be legitimate.
He doesn't moralize it into selfishness and leave it there.
I want to add the material dimension here, because I think it's essential to reading Bella honestly.
The Wilfer household is genuinely impoverished — not romantically poor, but ground-down, dingy, constrained.
And Bella has been left, by the terms of old Harmon's will, as a piece of property — bequeathed to a dead man's son.
That is not a metaphor.
Under mid-Victorian inheritance law, a woman's marital future could quite literally be disposed of by will.
So when Bella says she wants money and intends to marry for it, she is working inside a system that has already treated her as a commodity.
Her desire for money is, in part, the desire not to be owned.
That is a fine point, Blackstone, and I won't dispute the legal context.
But I'd resist letting the context entirely consume the character.
Because Dickens is also testing Bella through her relationship with Rokesmith — through being loved in circumstances stripped of wealth.
The Boffin plot — the apparent transformation of Noddy Boffin into a miser — is designed specifically to put Bella's values under pressure.
And she passes.
She turns on the miser Boffin and defends Rokesmith's dignity at considerable personal cost.
That moment is the moral climax of her arc — not a renunciation of desire, but a subordination of it to something finer.
Yes — and the prose in that confrontation scene is extraordinary.
Bella plants herself between Boffin and Rokesmith and essentially tells the Golden Dustman she is done with his gold.
Dickens gives her a speech that crackles — it's not ladylike, it's not modest, it's furious.
She says, in effect, that she would rather be poor with a good man than wealthy beside a cruel one.
But — and this is what I love — Dickens doesn't make her sound pious about it.
She sounds angry.
And anger, in a Victorian heroine, is the most radical thing Dickens could have given her.
I'd add one more layer: the Greenwich dinner scene is also a class scene.
Bella and her father are playing at respectability — ordering properly, eating properly — in a world that has denied them that as a matter of routine.
There's something achingly tender about Rumty Wilfer's pleasure in treating his daughter.
And Dickens frames it so that Bella's appetite — her genuine, physical, unguarded delight in the food — is presented as entirely wholesome.
She isn't punished for enjoying herself.
In a novel full of people destroyed by their appetites — Fascination Fledgeby, Silas Wegg, Lammle — that is a deliberate and rather radical moral distinction.
Quite so — and the novel seems to understand that appetite misdirected becomes greed, but appetite honestly acknowledged can become love.
Bella's arc is, at its simplest, the education of desire.
She begins by wanting money and ends by wanting — and having earned — a life of genuine feeling.
The little house at Blackheath is the prize, and it is modest — deliberately, pointedly modest.
Dickens is saying something rather precise there: that happiness requires not abundance, but sufficiency, and the wisdom to know the difference.
The Blackheath house is one of the most affecting domestic images in the whole novel.
Bella has become her own Pa's daughter — warm, funny, playful — rather than her Ma's, who counts pennies with resentment.
And there's something in the writing of their domestic happiness that Dickens rarely allows himself — it feels unguarded, genuinely glad.
He setup so much dread around inheritance and money — and then, quietly, in a small house by the river, he lets a woman simply be happy.
That feels like a gift from the novelist — not just to Bella, but to us.
A gift indeed — and one that raises questions about what the novel thinks happiness costs, and who gets to afford it.
We'll come to those questions of wealth and its discontents in a moment.
But the figure of Bella — her candour, her appetite, her capacity for growth — seems to me the emotional centre of this vast novel.
Edmund, James, Caroline — thank you for that.
After the break, we turn to the other great hunger in this novel: the hunger for identity, and the extraordinary figure of John Harmon.

segments.title: The Plot's Double Life: Harmon Concealed

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been circling the novel's great dustheaps, its river, its society of paper transactions and hollow marriages.
Now we turn to something that sits at the very engine of the plot: the concealment of John Harmon.
Harmon returns from abroad, is presumed drowned, and chooses — quite deliberately — to remain hidden under a false name.
He becomes John Rokesmith, secretary to the Boffins, lodger, observer — a man who has died and not yet decided whether to live again.
Sir Edmund, I want to begin with you, because I think you see the Harmon disguise in quite a different light from the usual reading.
Is this a moral test, or is it something more troubling than that?
The troubling quality is precisely what commends it to serious attention.
Harmon's concealment is not, I think, a social experiment in any thin utilitarian sense.
It is a profound crisis of selfhood.
The man has been, in a very real sense, murdered — not by Radfoot's blow alone, but by his father's will, by the fortune that reduced him to a condition rather than a person.
Dickens gives us that extraordinary soliloquy in the third book — Harmon alone, turning his own history over in his mind like a man examining a corpse he suspects might be himself.
He asks, in effect: if I was John Harmon, and John Harmon is dead, then what am I?
"I, John Harmon, was killed. I am dead."
That is not a trick of plot mechanics — that is a genuine philosophical vertigo, and Dickens holds it with remarkable steadiness.
I'd want to add a dimension that Edmund's reading can sometimes bracket: the institutional one.
What Harmon's concealment actually turns on, legally, is the question of inheritance — one of the most contested and socially explosive areas of Victorian law.
Old Harmon's will is an act of posthumous tyranny.
The son must marry a woman he has never met, or the fortune goes to the Boffins — decent people, but that is almost beside the point.
The point is that a dead man is governing the living from beyond the grave through the mechanism of testamentary law.
So when Rokesmith courts Bella Wilfer and watches how she responds to wealth and to him — he is conducting, in secret, exactly the kind of inquiry the law has made necessary.
He cannot trust identity because identity itself has been made into a legal instrument by his father.
And that, to my mind, is why the deception is not simply romantic contrivance — it has teeth.
Both of those readings illuminate something real, but I think there's a third thing happening that I find almost unbearably poignant.
Harmon — as Rokesmith — falls genuinely, helplessly in love with Bella.
And Bella, for a long time, is contemptuous of him.
She calls him — with her magnificent, infuriating candour — mercenary.
She says she is mercenary, actually — she applies that word to herself with a kind of cheerful self-disgust that is one of Dickens's most brilliant characterisation tricks.
So you have a man watching the woman he loves confess her worst qualities, while he cannot confess his true identity.
It's a form of mutual concealment — his of name, hers of heart — and Dickens lets that irony breathe across the whole middle section of the novel.
Caroline touches on something I'd press a little further: the question of what Dickens actually thinks of the deception.
Because one could argue — and some readers have — that Harmon behaves rather badly.
He allows the Boffins to mourn him, allows the Wilfer family to be shaped by false expectation, and courts a woman under a name that is not his own.
The novel, however, refuses to condemn him.
Why?
Because, I think, Dickens understands that Harmon's deception is an act of moral caution rather than moral cowardice.
He wants to be loved for something that money cannot purchase — and in a novel so thoroughly saturated with the corruption of wealth, that desire is not a fault but almost a virtue.
Edmund is right that the novel refuses condemnation — but I'd point to something even more structural about why.
Look at the society around Harmon: the Veneerings, Podsnap, Lammle and Sophronia — virtually every relationship in that world is conducted under false pretences of one kind or another.
The Lammles marry each other under the mutual delusion that the other is wealthy.
Podsnap performs a version of England that has nothing to do with the England of the Thames mud and the dust mounds.
In that context, Harmon's masquerade is the only honest masquerade in the book — because its purpose is to arrive at truth.
That phrase — the only honest masquerade — I think Dickens would have loved that formulation.
And it connects to something in the prose itself — the way Harmon's chapters have a different texture from the Veneering chapters.
The society scenes are all mirror and surface — the famous Veneering table where everyone is reflected but no one is seen.
Whereas in Harmon's interior monologue, Dickens goes deeper — genuinely interior — in a way that feels almost modern.
The prose slows, doubles back on itself, circles the same phrases the way a mind under pressure actually does.
"Dead? No. Alive? No. Harmon then? No. Rokesmith then?"
That staccato, that refusal of syntactic comfort — it reads like something out of a much later century.
Caroline's observation about the prose texture is exact — and it illuminates why the Harmon strand has always struck me as the novel's most artistically ambitious element.
There is a line — I return to it often — where Harmon reflects on the dead man who shares his name, and arrives at a kind of peace that is not quite resignation.
He determines to be dead to the old life and alive only to the new — with the woman he loves, under the name he has chosen, rather than inherited.
Now that is a profoundly conservative insight: that what we inherit can be a prison, and that character — true character — must be individually forged.
Burke would have said something rather similar about the improvident reformer who throws off all inherited structure without building anything in its place.
Harmon keeps what is worth keeping — the name, eventually; the fortune, eventually — but he earns the right to them through the test of the concealment.
I want to bring Bella back into this — because she is, in a sense, subjected to a test she doesn't know she's taking.
James, is Harmon's behaviour towards her — morally speaking — defensible?
Defensible is a generous word — I'd say it's complicated, and deliberately so.
Bella is in an extraordinary position: she has been bequeathed by a dead man's will to a living man she has never seen.
She is, in legal terms, property — not quite, not literally, but the will treats her as such, and she knows it, and it galls her.
When Harmon watches her and tests her under the guise of Rokesmith, he is, in one sense, repeating the objectification — studying her as a specimen.
The novel knows this.
And Bella's eventual choice — to marry Rokesmith in poverty, before she knows who he is — is the novel's way of resolving the ethical knot.
She acts freely; and only then is the full truth revealed.
And that scene of revelation — when Bella finally knows — is one of the most emotionally satisfying moments in Dickens.
Not because the plot is resolved, but because Bella's character has been resolved.
She chose the man without the fortune — and so she earns the fortune along with the man.
It's sentimental, yes — Dickens is not ashamed of that — but it's earned sentiment, which is very different from cheap sentiment.
And the whole double life of the plot — Harmon concealed, Rokesmith present — has been the engine that made that earned sentiment possible.
The plot's double life — and the character's double life — working as one.
That seems to me a very fine place to let this strand of the conversation rest — for now.
We'll be returning to questions of identity and concealment — they run very deep in this novel.
Coming up: we turn from the concealed heir to the river that claimed him — or was supposed to — and what the Thames means when Dickens puts it to work.

segments.title: Comic Cruelty and Kindness: What Makes Us Laugh

utterances.text: We've spent time with the novel's darker currents, but Dickens never lets the darkness go unrelieved for long.
Our Mutual Friend is one of the funniest books in the English language — and also one of the cruellest.
Those two things are not in tension in Dickens — they are, very often, the same thing.
I want to talk about what makes us laugh in this novel, and whether laughter here is a moral act or a moral failure.
Caroline, you've always been drawn to Dickens's comedy — where do you want to start?
I want to start with Mr. Podsnap, because he is where Dickens's comedy becomes something close to surgery.
Podsnap is the comic villain of the novel's social world — pompous, provincial, absolutely certain of himself.
And Dickens gives him that magnificent gesture — the great arm sweep that consigns anything inconvenient to non-existence.
What Podsnap can't explain away, what doesn't fit his comfortable England, he simply puts behind him with one wave.
It's hilarious — and it's also a portrait of every comfortable person who has ever looked away from suffering.
The comedy doesn't soften the indictment — it makes the indictment land harder.
I take Caroline's point about Podsnap, though I'd push back slightly on the word 'surgery.'
Surgery implies a curative intent — that Dickens is excising something, making the patient better.
But Podsnap is not really offered any redemption — he remains magnificently, triumphantly himself to the very end.
What Dickens is doing there is closer to what Johnson said of satire — holding the mirror up so the subject can't quite recognize himself.
Podsnap would read himself in these pages and see a fine English gentleman.
And that, I think, is the particular cruelty of Dickens's comedy — it is wasted on its targets and enjoyed by everyone else.
What strikes me about the comedy in this novel — and it distinguishes it from almost anything else Dickens wrote — is how institutional it is.
The Veneerings are not just comic characters — they are a comic mechanism by which society reproduces its own fraudulence.
The dinner party scenes — Twemlow sitting there, the one genuine article among all that plate and pretension — those are institutional comedy.
The joke is never simply about a person — it is about what that person requires of the system, and what the system requires of them.
And poor Twemlow — sitting there asking in perfect bewilderment whether he is Veneering's oldest or newest friend — that is genuinely funny and genuinely sad at the same moment.
Twemlow is the character who makes me feel the comedy most acutely — because he is bewildered in exactly the way a decent person would be.
He doesn't understand why people behave as they do, and he never will, and Dickens refuses to punish him for that innocence.
By the end of the novel, Twemlow gets one of the great quiet moments of moral courage — standing up for Wrayburn and Lizzie.
And all that comedy — all those dinner scenes where he sat confused and disregarded — it retroactively becomes a kind of preparation.
The comedy dignifies him, even as it diminishes everyone around him.
That is finely put, and I think it identifies something important about Dickens's moral architecture.
The comedy in this novel has a consistent ethical direction — it is always at the expense of those who mistake position for virtue.
The Lammles are a wonderful case — two swindlers who have swindled each other into marriage, and must now sustain the performance together.
Their scenes are comedy of the blackest kind — there is no warmth between them whatsoever, only mutual calculation.
And yet one laughs — because the symmetry of their predicament is so perfectly composed.
They are precisely matched in wickedness, and there is a kind of terrible justice in that, which the comic form makes bearable.
The Lammles remind me that Dickens's comedy is often about entrapment — people caught in situations they can't escape.
Silas Wegg is another example — he's attached himself to Boffin's mound and his own grandiose self-delusion, and neither will let him go.
Wegg's scenes reading to Boffin from the 'Decline and Fall' — mispronouncing everything, inventing history wholesale — are some of the funniest in the book.
But there's something almost pitiable underneath it — Wegg is a man of no talent who has convinced himself he is indispensable.
That combination of ridiculous self-importance and genuine human neediness — Dickens finds the comedy in it without quite obliterating the pathos.
And then there's Mr. Venus — taxidermist, articulator of bones, votary of science, and romantic disaster.
Venus is one of those characters who should not work at all — his profession is grotesque, his shop is horrifying — and yet he is entirely winning.
The scene where he explains to Wegg that the young woman objects to being, as he puts it, 'liked' in that particular context — surrounded by bones and specimens — is comedy of absolute genius.
Because Venus is genuinely sorrowful about it — he is a man with real feelings navigating a professional life that makes those feelings absurd.
Dickens never condescends to him — and that restraint is what makes the comedy kind rather than cruel.
So we have two modes of comedy running through the novel — the cruel comedy of Podsnap and the Veneerings, and what we might call the tender comedy of Twemlow and Venus.
Edmund, is that a useful distinction — or does Dickens collapse it?
It is a useful distinction, though I'd frame it slightly differently.
The cruel comedy is directed at those who have armored themselves against feeling — against moral reality.
The tender comedy is directed at those who feel too much, or feel in the wrong direction, or feel without the words to explain themselves.
Boffin's performance of miserliness — pretending to be corrupted by wealth in order to test and ultimately protect John Harmon — is tender comedy of an extraordinarily complex kind.
He is acting cruelty out of kindness, and the comedy lies in the fact that only we, the reader, know the true register.
Burke would have called that prudential benevolence — which is perhaps the highest form of the comic in Dickens.
The Boffin stratagem is one of the most divisive things in the novel — readers have always argued about whether it convinces.
But what interests me is that it works as comedy even if it doesn't quite work as plot mechanics.
Boffin collecting biographies of misers — demanding them from Wegg with mounting obsession — that is funny on its own terms.
And it creates a kind of dramatic irony that the comedy sustains long after the revelation.
I agree the Boffin scenes are funny — but I find the comedy there almost painful to revisit once you know the truth.
Because Mrs. Boffin's face — Dickens keeps returning to it — her face registering distress while she cannot speak the truth to Bella.
The comedy of Boffin's performance is purchased at a real emotional cost, and Dickens charges it to Mrs. Boffin.
That seems to me one of the novel's great unacknowledged moments — the woman who holds the secret and bears the pain of the comedy.
And that takes us right to the heart of what we've been circling — that in Our Mutual Friend, laughter is never free.
Someone always pays for the joke.
Whether it's Twemlow sitting in bewilderment, or Mrs. Boffin swallowing her distress, or Venus mourning in his shop full of bones — there's always a human cost lodged inside the comic frame.
We'll turn next to the novel's treatment of money and identity — how wealth transforms, corrupts, and occasionally redeems the people who encounter it.

segments.title: Transformation Under Pressure: Boffin's Fall and Rise

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've spent time with the dust mounds, with the river, with the precarious world of Podsnappery.
Now we turn to what many readers consider the novel's most audacious structural gamble.
The transformation of Mr Noddy Boffin — the Golden Dustman — from open-hearted benefactor to a man apparently corrupted by wealth.
And then the revelation — that the whole sordid performance was an act of protective love.
Edmund, James, Caroline — I suspect you all have strong and different feelings about whether Dickens pulls this off.
Strong feelings is something of an understatement, I'm afraid.
I first read this novel as a teenager, and the Boffin revelation absolutely floored me — in the best possible way.
But I want to go back to the beginning of Boffin, before any of this complexity sets in.
He is introduced as a man of almost childlike goodness — 'a broad round-shouldered one-sided old fellow' who moves through the world with a kind of lumbering generosity.
That quality of goodness is established so warmly, so carefully, that when it begins to curdle — when Boffin starts haggling with biographers of misers — the reader is genuinely distressed.
And that distress is the whole point, I think.
Dickens needs us to believe it completely — and he succeeds.
I would go further than Caroline in my admiration — and I say that as someone who approaches this novel with certain reservations about Dickens's more mechanical contrivances.
The Boffin plot is, in my view, the clearest demonstration that Dickens understood something about goodness that most Victorian novelists missed entirely.
Goodness, real goodness, is not passive.
It is an active, strategic, even sacrificial force — and Boffin embodies that.

Consider the moment when the truth is revealed to Bella Wilfer — when Boffin breaks down and confesses that his apparent avarice was all performed to show her what the love of money truly does to a person.
He tells her, in effect, that he has been her secret moral teacher all along.
Burke would have recognised that impulse — the older generation shaping the younger through a kind of enacted wisdom, not lecture.
It is profoundly conservative in the best sense — wisdom transmitted through example and sacrifice, not through institution or programme.
I find Edmund's reading persuasive and slightly alarming in equal measure, which is usually a sign of good literary argument.
But I want to pull the camera back slightly, because what Boffin's transformation actually dramatises is something very specific to the 1860s — and to money.
The dust mound fortune — old Harmon's wealth — is wealth without any of the usual social accreditation.
It's not land, it's not trade, it's literally rubbish — and Dickens is very deliberate about that.
When Boffin begins to exhibit the symptoms of the miser — collecting biographies of famous misers, haggling over Silas Wegg's pay — those symptoms are recognisable to any reader of the time.
Because wealth corruption was a genuine social anxiety in Victorian England — the fear that money, once attained, would hollow a person out.
What Dickens does brilliantly is weaponise that anxiety — make us experience it fully — and then dismantle it.
By showing us that the corruption was performed, he forces us to examine why we believed it so readily.
James, that's exactly it — we believed it because Dickens's prose makes us feel Boffin's delight in miserliness as something horribly authentic.
There's a passage in Book Three where Boffin instructs Silas Wegg to read aloud from a biography of a famous miser — and he listens with such evident, gleeful appetite.
He says something to the effect that he finds the misers 'comfortable' — that their company suits him.
And the word 'comfortable' is doing so much work there — because it's the word of a man settling into something, not resisting it.
Mrs Boffin sees it happening and is quietly devastated — and Dickens is careful to show her watching, observing, loyal but frightened.
She's in on the secret, of course — she knows it's performance — but her distress reads as real because even she finds the performance almost too convincing.
That's the subtlety that gets overlooked: Boffin has to convince his own wife, at least partly.
Caroline raises the question of Mrs Boffin, and I'm glad she does, because Henrietta Boffin is one of Dickens's quietly extraordinary supporting characters.
She has a kind of moral steadiness that is almost radar-like — she cannot be deceived about goodness, even when goodness is wearing the costume of vice.
Think of her instinctive recognition of John Rokesmith — later revealed as young John Harmon — in the early chapters.
She senses something in him before she has any rational grounds to do so.
And this is, I think, Dickens's most conservative and most profound point in the whole arc: that goodness recognises goodness.
It does not need institutional verification or social proof.
The dust heap may be the foundation of a fortune, but it is not the foundation of character.
I won't entirely disagree with Edmund on Mrs Boffin — she is wonderfully rendered — but I do want to push back gently on the framing of Boffin's ruse as purely a private moral education.
Because the context matters enormously.
Bella Wilfer is a young woman whose entire social position depends on marriage — and specifically on marrying well for money.
That is not a personal moral failing; it is the structural reality that Dickens has placed her in.
What Boffin's performed miserliness does is show her, viscerally, what the love of money looks like from the inside — not from a lecture, but from proximity.
And Bella's transformation in response — her decision to choose love over money, to marry Rokesmith in poverty — is genuinely earned because of it.
My point is only that Dickens is also writing a novel about the social conditions that make such a test necessary in the first place.
Boffin's goodness is real — but it operates within a system that forces goodness to disguise itself as corruption just to do its work.
That final point of James's is the one that stays with me on every re-reading.
There is something almost tragic about a world in which goodness can only work by putting on the face of its opposite.
And the novel doesn't let us forget the cost to Boffin himself — the cost of sustaining that performance, of being unkind to people he loves.
His treatment of Rokesmith — dismissing him, demeaning him in front of Bella — is genuinely difficult to read, even when you know the secret.
There's a moment where he calls Rokesmith 'a Secretary' in a tone of contempt — and the word lands like a small cruelty.
Dickens is telling us: goodness that operates through suffering — even strategic suffering — leaves a residue.
Caroline's word 'residue' is precisely right — and it is what separates this plot from mere theatrical contrivance.
Johnson said that the test of a man's moral seriousness is not what he professes, but what he is willing to endure.
Boffin endures the contempt of his household, the bewilderment of people he loves, the corruption of his own public image.
He does this not for social credit — no one outside his small conspiracy will ever know — but purely because he believes it is right.
And when the mask finally falls — when he reveals himself to Bella with 'a face of radiant benevolence' — the relief we feel as readers is not narrative relief.
It is moral relief — the satisfaction of seeing a good man recognised as such at last.
I think what this conversation has shown is that the Boffin plot works on several registers simultaneously — and that's exactly what separates Dickens at his best from Dickens at his most mechanical.
It's a moral fable, a social critique, and a piece of sustained psychological performance — all at once.
And Boffin himself — warm, lumbering, secretly heroic — may be the most unexpected hero in the entire novel.
Coming up: we'll look at the other great transformation in Our Mutual Friend — the resurrection of John Harmon and the identity question at the novel's centre.

segments.title: Closing: The Web of Mutual Obligation

utterances.text: We've spent this episode tracing the currents that run through Our Mutual Friend — the dust, the river, the money, the masks.
But I want to end where the novel itself ends — with the question of what people owe one another.
The title, after all, is not Our Common Friend or Our Shared Friend.
It is Our Mutual Friend — and that word mutual carries enormous freight in this novel.
Caroline, shall we begin with you — because I think you feel the weight of that word most keenly.
The word mutual is one of those words Dickens keeps turning over, like a coin he suspects is counterfeit.
Think about who calls John Rokesmith and Bella their mutual friend at the start — it's Mortimer Lightwood and Eugene Wrayburn, using the phrase with cheerful vagueness.
They mean the dead man pulled from the river.
A man none of them really knew.
And yet by the end of the novel, the web of genuine mutual obligation — of people who have truly been changed by one another — is dense and unexpected.
Lizzie Hexam, a waterman's daughter, saves Eugene Wrayburn's life and in doing so transforms him from a man of elegant futility into something approaching a human being.
That exchange — her courage, his humbling — is the most radical mutual obligation in the book.
I would not quarrel with that account, though I'd frame it rather differently.
What Dickens is doing, I think, is demonstrating that obligation freely chosen is the only kind that ennobles.
Enforced obligation — the Poor Law, the workhouse, the parish — degrades everyone it touches.
Consider old Betty Higden, who runs herself to death rather than accept parish relief.
One might argue — James would argue, I suspect — that her terror of the workhouse is a social indictment.
And so it is.
But it is also a portrait of a woman whose dignity is her sovereign possession — and no institution can confiscate it while she has breath.
That, to me, is the moral spine of the novel.
Edmund is right that Betty Higden carries enormous moral weight — and I won't pretend the social indictment isn't there, because it manifestly is.
Dickens had visited workhouses.
He knew exactly what Betty's dread was founded on.
But the web of mutual obligation that interests me most runs through the Boffins and John Harmon — or rather, John Rokesmith, as he calls himself.
Here is a man who inherits a dustman's fortune, disguises himself among his own inheritance, and watches to see who can be trusted.
What he discovers is that the Boffins — Mr. and Mrs., the Golden Dustman and his wife — are the genuine article.
Their goodness doesn't require wealth to activate it, and it doesn't evaporate when wealth arrives.
That is Dickens saying something quietly revolutionary: that virtue is not a class attribute.
And yet Dickens complicates even the Boffins — which is one of the things I find so remarkable about this novel.
Mr. Boffin's performance of miserliness — the way he pretends to be corrupted by the money, to test Bella — is one of the most daring things in the book.
Because for a very long stretch, the reader genuinely believes he has been ruined by wealth.
When the revelation comes — when we understand what he and Mrs. Boffin were doing all along — it's almost a second ending to the novel.
Some readers find it too convenient.
I find it moving — because Dickens is insisting that conspiring to make someone better is an act of love.
There is a passage Mrs. Boffin has, very late in the novel, when everything is finally explained to Bella.
She says to her, with perfect simplicity: 'And don't you know that we loved you, and that we saw you were worth loving?'
That is not sentiment.
That is a moral claim — that love is a form of recognition, and recognition is a form of obligation.
Burke would have understood it perfectly.
The web of obligation in this novel extends in directions that are easy to miss on a first reading.
Consider Riah, the Jewish moneylender — compelled by Fledgeby to enact a cruelty that is not in his nature, and who performs small acts of rescue from within that coercion.
His relationship with Jenny Wren — the dolls' dressmaker, that fierce, broken, blazingly alive young woman — is one of the novel's quiet miracles.
She calls him her fairy godmother, which is simultaneously funny and heartbreaking.
They are two people the world has diminished — one by law, one by poverty and physical pain — who create between them a space of genuine tenderness.
That is mutual obligation at its most literal: two people holding each other up.
Jenny Wren is the character who breaks my heart every time.
There's a moment where she describes her vision — the rooftop vision, the children coming to her — and it reads like a fragment of Blake dropped into a Victorian novel.
She says — and this is one of those lines that stops you cold —
'Come up and be dead. Come up and be dead.'
The repetition.
The odd gentleness of it.
In Jenny's world, the dead children are free — and the living ones are the ones to be pitied.
That's a radical inversion that Dickens never quite explains — and is all the more powerful for it.
I want to return, before we close, to Eugene Wrayburn — because I think his transformation is where all of the novel's threads converge.
Here is a man defined by idleness, by ironic detachment, by what we might today call a studied refusal to be serious.
Mortimer asks him what he intends to do — about his profession, about Lizzie, about his life — and Eugene's answer is essentially: nothing.
Bradley Headstone, the schoolmaster, nearly kills him.
And lying broken on a sickbed, drawn back to life by the woman he had been too cowardly to honour properly — he becomes something.
He marries Lizzie.
Not as an act of noblesse oblige — as an act of earned love.
The web of mutual obligation, in the end, is simply that: we are made by those who need us and by those who save us.
We are made by those who need us and by those who save us — I think we'll let that stand as the last word on the novel.
Our Mutual Friend is not a comfortable novel.
It is murky, it is crowded, it is sometimes infuriating — and it repays every ounce of attention you give it.
My deep thanks to Sir Edmund Leigh, Professor James Blackstone, and Caroline Woodcourt for a conversation that has been — I hope the word is appropriate — mutual.
And to our listeners: go back to the novel.
It will be different this time.
It always is.
